title: What is a 1099-INT form? Reporting interest income
summary: What is a 1099-INT form? Learn how interest income is reported, who gets one, the threshold, and what to do at tax time. Read on.
body_markdown:
A little extra money in a savings account can feel like a welcome reward, especially when it has been earning interest throughout the year while you're saving for a house, building an emergency fund, or simply setting some money aside for unexpected expenses. When January arrives, however, the bank may send a tax document showing exactly how much interest that money generated, leaving you wondering whether those earnings are taxable, whether they need to appear on your tax return, and what happens if the amount is relatively small.


This is where Form 1099-INT comes in. So, what is a 1099-INT form, and why does a bank send one? It is an IRS tax document used to report interest income paid to you by banks, credit unions, brokerage firms, and other financial institutions during the tax year. Generally, the payer must issue it when reportable interest reaches $10, although certain exceptions apply.


The form provides a record of your interest earnings and helps the IRS verify the income reported on your tax return, but receiving one does not mean the entire amount is an additional tax bill. Even when the interest seems insignificant, or no form arrives, taxable interest may still need to be reported. Understanding what a 1099-INT form is can help you know when to expect one, what the reporting threshold means, and how to include your interest income when filing your taxes.


## **What is a 1099-INT form?**


Form 1099-INT is an IRS information return that reports interest income paid to you during the calendar year. If money in a bank account, certificate of deposit, or investments earns interest, the institution or organisation that pays it may send you this form. It gives you and the IRS a record of the interest to include on your federal tax return, even without a withdrawal.


### Who issues Form 1099-INT?


Banks, credit unions, brokerage firms, and other organisations that pay interest issue Form 1099-INT when IRS reporting rules apply. A payer must send it if it paid you at least $10 in reportable interest during the year. A form may also be required for amounts below $10, such as when federal income tax was withheld. The payer sends a copy to you and the IRS.


### What types of interest does it cover?


The form can report interest from savings and checking accounts, savings accounts, certificates of deposit (CDs), and money market deposit accounts. It can also include interest from bonds and U.S. Treasury securities, along with other debt investments. The source and amount are generally shown in separate boxes.


Receiving Form 1099-INT does not mean you owe tax on every dollar shown. Most bank interest is taxable, while qualifying tax-exempt interest is treated differently but may still need to be reported. You generally must report taxable interest even if you did not withdraw it or receive a form.


## **Who gets a 1099-INT?**


Anyone who earns $10 or more in reportable interest during a calendar year will generally receive Form 1099-INT from the bank or financial institution that paid them. This $10 threshold remains unchanged for the 2026 tax year. It applies to people earning interest from savings accounts, fixed-term deposits, and certain investments.


### Who may receive the form?


You may receive a 1099-INT if you have a savings account, certificate of deposit (CD), money market account, or bonds that pay interest. Your bank or financial institution sends you a copy and reports the same earnings to the IRS. If you're unfamiliar with the wider 1099 series, understanding[what a 1099 form is](http://grey.co/blog/what-is-a-1099) also helps explain why different types of income have separate reporting forms.


### **What if you earn less than $10?**


If your interest is below $10, you may not receive a 1099-INT. However, the bank must still send one if it took federal tax from your interest or paid foreign tax on your behalf, even when the amount is lower.


Remember, the $10 limit only determines when the bank must send the form. It does not mean smaller interest payments are tax-free. You must still report taxable interest on your tax return, even if you never receive a 1099-INT. The[IRS explains the reporting rules for Form 1099-INT](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-1099-int) , including when banks must send it.


## **Reporting interest income**


All taxable interest must be reported on your federal tax return, even if you did not receive Form 1099-INT. This means that if your bank paid you interest during the year, you still need to include it when filing your taxes, whether the amount was $5 or $500. Leaving the money in your account instead of withdrawing it does not make the interest tax-free.


### **How to report interest without Form 1099-INT**


Start by checking your year-end bank statements to see how much interest you earned across your accounts. Add the amounts together and include the total taxable interest when preparing your federal tax return. Keep your statements as proof of the payments in case the IRS asks for more information.


### **When do you need Schedule B?**


If your total taxable interest is more than $1,500, you generally need to complete an additional tax form called Schedule B and submit it with your federal tax return. This form lists the banks and other organisations that paid you interest. Other situations, including certain foreign account interests, may also require it.


Tax-exempt interest, such as interest from qualifying municipal bonds, is reported separately from ordinary taxable interest. Some investment funds also pay tax-exempt dividends, which are reported differently from bank interest. You can learn more about[what a 1099-DIV reports](http://grey.co/blog/what-is-a-1099-div) to understand how investment income is recorded.


This information is for general educational purposes and is not professional tax advice. Check the relevant IRS instructions or speak with a tax professional about your circumstances.


## Interest income and foreign accounts


Earning interest from a bank outside the US does not mean it is automatically exempt from US taxes. If you are a US citizen or resident alien, you generally need to report taxable interest from foreign accounts, just as you would interest earned from a US bank. This applies even if the foreign bank does not send you Form 1099-INT. Keep your bank statements so you can work out how much interest you earned and report the amount in US dollars.

## Frequently asked questions about the Form 1099-INT


### What is a 1099-INT used for?


Form 1099-INT reports interest income paid to you during the tax year by banks, credit unions, brokerage firms, and other financial institutions. The payer sends a copy to you and the IRS, showing how much interest you earned. You use this information when preparing your federal income tax return.


### What is the 1099-INT threshold?


Banks and other financial institutions generally issue Form 1099-INT when they pay you $10 or more in interest during the calendar year. The form may also be required below this amount if federal income tax or foreign tax was withheld. Remember, the $10 threshold does not make smaller interest payments tax-free.


### Do I report interest without a 1099-INT?


Yes. You must report taxable interest on your federal tax return even if you earned less than $10 and never received Form 1099-INT. Check your year-end bank statements and add up the interest earned across your accounts. The responsibility to report taxable interest remains yours, whether or not the bank sends a form.


### Is interest income taxable?


Most interest income is taxable at your ordinary federal income tax rate, including earnings from savings accounts, certificates of deposit, and money market accounts. However, some interest, such as qualifying interest from municipal bonds, is federally tax-exempt. You may still need to report tax-exempt interest separately when filing your federal tax return.


### What about interest from foreign accounts?


US citizens and resident aliens generally must report taxable interest earned from foreign bank accounts, even if they do not receive Form 1099-INT. Depending on the total value of their foreign accounts and other circumstances, they may also need to file an FBAR or Form 8938. These are separate reporting requirements.


### When should I receive my 1099-INT?


Banks and other financial institutions generally send Form 1099-INT by January 31 following the tax year in which you earned the interest. If the deadline falls on a weekend or public holiday, it moves to the next business day. Check your email, online banking account, or post for the document.


### What should I do if my 1099-INT has incorrect information?


Contact the bank or financial institution that issued the form and ask for a corrected copy. Compare the reported amount with your bank statements to identify any differences. If the institution confirms the error, request that it send the corrected form to both you and the IRS before you file your tax return.
